This report serves as both a testament to the achieve-
ments of female founders and a call to action for all stake-
holders in the entrepreneurial ecosystem. It highlights the 
importance of fostering an inclusive environment where 
diverse voices can thrive. By amplifying these findings 
and stories, we hope to inspire collaboration, mentor-
ship, and investment in women-led ventures. Supporting 
female founders is about unlocking opportunities that 
contribute to economic development and social change. 
Together, let us champion the spirit of female 
entrepreneurship and work towards a future where 
every aspiring founder has the opportunity to succeed, 
regardless of gender.
In an era where innovation and entrepreneurship are more 
vital than ever, the voices of female founders are emerging 
as powerful catalysts for change. This report highlights 
the remarkable journeys of women who have not only 
broken barriers but have also redefined the landscape of 
business and leadership.
As we delve into the survey findings, case studies and 
insights shared within these pages, we recognise the 
unique challenges faced by female entrepreneurs—
challenges that often stem from systemic biases and 
societal expectations. Yet, despite these hurdles, women 
continue to rise, innovate, and inspire. Their resilience 
and creativity are not just reshaping industries; they are 
paving the way for future generations of leaders.
The findings also emphasise the importance of a more in-
clusive environment. This is not simply about addressing 
inequalities but about recognising the value that diverse 
perspectives bring to innovation and problem-solving. 
By understanding these experiences and the broader 
patterns they reveal, stakeholders can better support 
an environment where all entrepreneurs have the 
potential to thrive. Investors, policymakers, mentors, and 
industry leaders have a role to play in fostering a more 
equitable landscape.

Female-founded businesses are a vital and dynamic 
force within the UK’s entrepreneurial landscape. As of 
October 2024, there are 7,696 high-growth companies 
in the UK with at least one female founder, representing 
13.7% of the country’s high-growth ecosystem. Female-
led enterprises contribute significantly to the nation’s 
economy, with high-growth female-founded businesses 
employing approximately 330k people across the UK.
There remains a need to improve female business 
leaders’ access to funding and empower them to create 
companies in industries that have strong investment 
potential. By supporting female founders in building 
scalable, high-growth businesses, we can expect to see 
a greater share of female-founded companies receiving 
equity investment, bringing this more in line with their 
male-founded counterparts.
Female founders tend to be between 30 and 40 years 
old when the business is founded, likely because 
entrepreneurs of this age have more business experience 
and are often more financially stable. There are, however, 
plenty of younger women starting businesses between 
the ages of 20 and 30. For these young entrepreneurs, the 
discrimination associated with being a female founder is 
even more pronounced.

In today’s business landscape, female-led businesses 
in the UK represent an underserved segment—facing 
funding gaps, limited networks, and biases, which may 
restrict their growth. A business is classified as female-
led if at least one woman is present in the founding team. 
If women make up more than half of the founders, the 
business is considered predominantly female-led.
 
As of October 2024, there are 7,696 high-growth 
companies with at least one female founder in the 
UK, representing 13.7% of the UK’s high-growth 
company population. Of these, 4,224 are predominantly 
female-founded.
Funding remains one of the most significant challenges 
for female-founded businesses, with survey findings 
revealing that only 24.8% of women believe it is easier to 
secure funding as a woman than a man. More than half 
(55.2%) of respondents also shared they feel they are 
under increased scrutiny due to their gender. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
In the first three quarters of 2024, female-founded 
companies have raised a collective £1.48b in equity 
funding via 972 deals. Though significant, this figure 
is overshadowed by the resources flowing into male-
led ventures. During the same period, businesses 
without female founders secured £9.28b—over six 
times the amount raised by female-founded businesses.

These figures highlight the higher share of equity 
flowing into male-led firms within the high-growth sector 
compared to female-led ones. This imbalance may stem 
from a range of factors, including the limited availability of 
equity finance, mentorship, and networking opportunities 
for women entrepreneurs. Increasing diversity within 
investment teams, for instance, could help address 
funding gaps, as research shows that female investors 
are more likely to support female founders.1
The disparity in representation has catalysed a growing 
need for initiatives that support and scale female-
led 
businesses. 
UK-based 
accelerators 
such 
as 
AccelerateHer focus specifically on fostering female 
entrepreneurship. Powered by Barclays Eagle Labs and 
funded by the UK government, AccelerateHer provides 
female founders in Scotland with free courses, in-person 
and virtual bootcamps, and targeted mentorship, aimed 
at accelerating business growth and enhancing visibility. 
The number of female-founded businesses has more 
than doubled over the past decade and continues to grow. 
As this trend accelerates, scaling support for female-
led companies will be crucial. From investment and 
mentorship programmes to diversity within investment 
firms, the business ecosystem stands to gain considerably 
from greater gender equality, resulting in a stronger, more 
resilient economy powered by diverse leadership.

Female business owners in the UK are fostering mutual 
success despite the challenges they face. According 
to the Charles Stanley Fortune Favours Survey, 70.8% of 
the 250 female respondents want to support other 
women in business, while 72.8% aimed to mentor young 
business leaders. The survey, conducted among 500 
UK business owners aged 18 and over with household 
incomes of at least £100k, included several questions 
directed exclusively at the 250 female participants. 
These questions focused on business topics, such as 
exit strategies and succession planning, as well as family 
financial dynamics and perceived challenges facing 
female business leaders.
Despite ongoing obstacles, 67.2% of female respondents 
reported feeling a responsibility to support peers within 
their industries. Notably, 46.0% agreed that starting 
a business today is easier than when they began, 
compared to 18.4% who disagreed, indicating that strides 
have been made towards a more inclusive business 
environment for women. 
Only 8.40% of respondents indicated that they would 
become angel investors. This may be a result of female 
entrepreneurs having less access to capital, wealth 
accumulation, and established networks, which in turn

investor (8.40%), a trustee (7.60%), or an employee at 
another business (6.40%).

Debbie Wosskow OBE is a British entrepreneur and angel 
investor known for promoting female entrepreneurship. 
Her entrepreneurial journey started early, marked by 
winning an enterprise award at the age of 15. Wosskow’s 
early experiences sparked her interest in business and 
helped shape her future career path. In 2011, she co-
founded Love Home Swap, a home exchange platform 
inspired by the film The Holiday. The platform enabled 
users to exchange homes for holidays. By 2017, it had 
grown to include over 100k homes across the world. 
Wosskow sold the business to Wyndham Destination 
Networks for £40.0m in 2017.
Alongside her entrepreneurial ventures, Wosskow has 
focused on supporting women in business. Drawing from 
her own experiences with the challenges women face 
in business, Wosskow co-founded AllBright in 2017—a 
network and resource platform dedicated to supporting 
women entrepreneurs through mentorship, networking, 
and educational programmes. For example, AllBright 
provides access to a digital academy offering courses on 
leadership, financial literacy, and investment readiness, 
helping female founders build the necessary skills to 
grow their businesses. Through AllBright, Wosskow aims 
to address the ongoing challenges that female founders 
face in securing funding and support. She explains: “We 
need to empower more women with the confidence to 
raise capital and equip them with the resources they need 
to do that effectively.” 2

In 2001, Tamara Lohan and her husband, James Lohan 
experienced a less-than-inspiring getaway at a spa in 
England’s Lake District. Frustrated by the lack of high-
quality and unique accommodations, the couple identified 
a gap in the market for discerning travellers seeking 
boutique hotel experiences. This insight led them to 
launch Mr & Mrs Smith in 2003—initially as a guidebook 
to boutique hotels. The company is named with a nod 
to the alias traditionally used by couples checking into 
hotels incognito.
After launching in 2003, Mr & Mrs Smith quickly resonated 
with an audience seeking curated recommendations. 
The first version of their guide sold 10,000 copies within 
six weeks, eventually surpassing 100,000.5 Recognising 
the potential of the internet, Lohan led the company’s 
digital transformation in 2005, transitioning from print to 
an online platform. The shift positioned Mr & Mrs Smith 
as a key destination for those seeking travel advice and 
booking boutique accommodation online.
Under Lohan’s leadership as Chief Technology Officer 
and later CEO, the business expanded its portfolio beyond 
hotels to include villas and exclusive travel experiences. 
By 2023, Mr & Mrs Smith boasted of over one million 
and featured more than 1,800 properties worldwide. The 
brand’s emphasis on personalised service and quality 
curation distinguished it from traditional travel agencies. 
“Every single one of our hotels is unique—they’re not 
cookie cutter,” noted Lohan in a recent interview.6
In May 2023 Hyatt Hotels acquired Mr & Mrs Smith for 
£53m. Lohan remained at the helm as CEO to guide 
the integration while preserving the brand’s distinctive 
ethos. The acquisition enabled the company to leverage 
Hyatt’s resources to enhance its offerings further and 
reach new markets. Beyond her executive role, Lohan 
has transitioned into advisory positions, sharing her 
entrepreneurial acumen as a Non-Executive Director 
(NED) at Fortnum & Mason since June 2023. Her expertise 
in technology and marketing strategy contributes to the 
storied retailer’s evolution in the digital age. She has also 
held a NED role at adventure travel firm Much Better 
Adventures since June 2021.

Martha Lane Fox rose to prominence in the late 1990s 
as the co-founder of Lastminute.com, an online travel 
and gift retailer specialising in distressed inventory. 
Founded in 1998 with Brent Hoberman, the company 
became emblematic of the dot-com boom. By January 
2000, Lastminute.com had hundreds of thousands of 
regular users; its initial public offering (IPO) in March 
2000 saw its valuation hit £571m. Despite the dot-com 
bust that followed, Lane Fox’s leadership during this 
period cemented her status as a leading figure in the UK’s 
internet economy.
Following her departure from Lastminute.com in 2003, 
Lane Fox continued to play an active role in the UK’s 
entrepreneurial landscape. She co-founded Lucky Voice 
in 2005, redefining karaoke in the UK. As the UK’s Digital 
Champion from 2009 to 2013, she led the Race Online 2012 
campaign to bring millions more Britons online. In 2015, 
she founded Doteveryone, advocating for responsible 
technology. Appointed to the House of Lords in 2013 
as a crossbench peer, she became its youngest female 
member. Lane Fox has a portfolio of responsibilities, 
including serving as Chancellor of the Open University, 
acting as a non-executive director at Chanel, and 
President of the British Chambers of Commerce.
Lane Fox’s life took a dramatic turn in 2004 when a severe 
car accident in Morocco left her with lasting disabilities. 
Demonstrating remarkable resilience, she adapted to her 
new circumstances and channelled her experiences into 
philanthropic efforts. She is a patron of Day One Trauma 
Support, a charity providing help to those affected by 
major trauma. Her philanthropic endeavours extend 
through Antigone, a grant-making trust she established 
in 2007 to support UK charities in healthcare, education, 
criminal justice, and technology. Lane Fox’s dedication to

Entrepreneurs and sisters Eccie and Gini Newton founded 
Karma Cans in 2014 as a corporate catering company, 
providing meals to offices across London. Inspired by 
Mumbai’s dabbawala system, their concept involved 
delivering fresh, home-cooked lunches in reusable 
containers. This focus on sustainability and convenience 
made their service popular among corporate workers in 
the City.
As Karma Cans grew, the Newtons encountered logistical 
challenges, particularly around kitchen space. To manage 
increasing demand, they moved from a home kitchen to 
a larger facility. This experience highlighted an issue in 
the food industry: limited access to affordable, flexible 
commercial kitchen space. Realising that other small food 
businesses faced similar challenges, the sisters decided 
to address this issue with a new venture.
In 2018, the Newtons launched Karma Kitchen, a co-
working kitchen space designed to provide small food 
businesses with affordable, flexible access to commercial 
kitchens. By offering shared, rentable kitchen spaces, 
Karma Kitchen helps reduce the financial burden of 
owning or leasing a private kitchen facility. This model 
allows emerging food businesses to operate more 
sustainably and food entrepreneurs to focus on growing 
their businesses rather than worrying about the high cost 
of infrastructure.
As an experienced founder, Eccie advises other women 
pursuing entrepreneurship by saying: “The one thing I’d 
say to female entrepreneurs is to create your own space, 
one that suits you. Do your own thing early, and don’t try 
to conform too much to a workplace that wasn’t really 
created or designed for you [as women], because that 
can take away some of your self-confidence.”9 Eccie also 
highlights another challenge for female founders, “There 
are not very many female founders in the UK that receive 
funding. There is a large intersectional group of people 
who contribute to the economy, who are consumers and 
members of our community, who are ignored when it 
comes to funding.”10

The journey of female entrepreneurship in the UK 
continues to be marked by resilience, ambition, and a 
growing sense of community. This report has explored the 
significant contributions female founders make to the UK 
economy, as well as the barriers they still face. 
Despite making up only 13.7% of the UK’s high-growth 
company 
population, 
female-founded 
businesses 
employ over 300k people and have received £1.48b in 
equity funding in 2024. Yet, prejudice still exists towards 
women in businesses, and the challenges are even more 
pronounced for younger entrepreneurs who are building 
their networks and establishing their reputations. 
The findings of the Charles Stanley Survey highlight the 
determination and support among female entrepreneurs.
The strong network across female leaders is crucial 
as the UK works to create a more inclusive business 
environment. However, sexism and increased scrutiny 
persist, underscoring the need for systemic change.
Conclusion
Barriers that prevent women from entering the entre-
preneurial landscape result in missed opportunities 
for new businesses and founders from a demographic 
that represents half of the UK population. 
Addressing these issues is more than a matter of fairness; 
it is an economic imperative. Greater investment in 
female-founded businesses and increasing diversity 
within investment firms can drive innovation, resilience, 
and economic growth. Initiatives like AccelerateHer 
and efforts by angel investors and advocates, such as 
Debbie Wosskow and Tamara Lohan, play a pivotal role in 
increasing diversity and inclusion. They demonstrate the 
tangible benefits of diverse leadership, which extends 
beyond gender and encompasses varied backgrounds 
and experiences.
Seeking professional advice, planning ahead and gaining 
access to long-term support can be the difference 
between entrepreneurial success and failure. Charles 
Stanley offers a comprehensive suite of services designed 
to meet the needs of entrepreneurs at every stage of 
their journey – from founding a business to succession 
planning and exiting.
As female entrepreneurship gains momentum, the UK 
stands at a crossroads. Continued progress will require 
sustained commitment from policymakers, investors, 
and industry leaders. By creating an ecosystem that 
empowers women at every stage—from launching 
startups to scaling and exiting businesses—the UK can 
unlock the full potential of its female founders. This not 
only benefits the women themselves but enriches the 
entire high-growth sectors, laying the foundation for a 
more inclusive and innovative future.
The vast majority 
of women are 
committed to 
mentoring and 
uplifting their peers.
